teaser: A bridge closure simulated on a story vault: newsworthy on 5 days, needed on 57, used by three readers, four buyers and an agent, and paid back to its sources.
core_idea: Played out as a simulation on a story vault, one local bridge closure shows the value of journalism as getting a disputed fact right and keeping it right: newsworthy on five days but needed on fifty-seven, used through Reader Skills by readers whose own graphs meet the story graph at shared anchors and who decide better with it, bought by institutions and agents who need the same claims, cheaper for agents than searching, and paid for in small amounts that walk back down the claims to the reporter, the paper and the residents whose evidence the graph names.

nodes.label: A bridge closes; the council says one week
nodes.summary: A fictional town's main crossing shuts for urgent repairs; the official estimate is a week.

nodes.label: The journalism is getting the date right
nodes.summary: The contract says three weeks, the engineer five to seven; the reporter finds both and the paper runs the contradiction.

nodes.label: Each correction supersedes the last
nodes.summary: The graph keeps every estimate with its date, so it can say what was believed on any day and why.

nodes.label: Newsworthy on five days, needed on fifty-seven
nodes.summary: The paper leads with the story five times; readers need its current state every day it is closed.

nodes.label: Each reader's graph meets the story
nodes.summary: Home, school, routes and customers held on the reader's device, joined to the claims at shared anchors.

nodes.label: A parent, a café owner, a plumber
nodes.summary: The same claims become a walking route, a stock plan and a job schedule.

nodes.label: Better decisions, counted
nodes.summary: A club booked in time, £640 of stock not wasted, £1,200 of relief claimed, nine hours of driving saved.

nodes.label: Without it: stale pages, rumours, nobody accountable
nodes.summary: The council page says a week for nine days, a group says Friday, TV covers day one and day forty-six.

nodes.label: Buyers who do not read the paper
nodes.summary: Highways teams, investors and national desks need the same graph for regional and national decisions.

nodes.label: Agents spend less and are right
nodes.summary: Searching costs about $377 over the closure and finds the stale page; asking the newsroom costs about $54.

nodes.label: £2,707, walked back to the sources
nodes.summary: Small amounts from 1,596 readers and businesses plus institutions; 35% to the reporter, £203 to a resident.

nodes.label: The simulation as a vault
nodes.summary: Every figure computed from written assumptions by a build script, published with its read key.

quotes.text: An article is written once. A maintained claim, kept current until the bridge opens, is a service.
quotes.why: Why the value of a local story outlives its news cycle.

quotes.text: As agents start planning school runs, deliveries and site visits for people, the cheapest thing they can buy is an accurate, maintained, accountable source.
quotes.why: Why agents should pay for local journalism.

figures.caption: The Wendmouth Courier on 2 November, in the simulation: the headline is one projection of the story graph, and the tracker beside it shows every source's reopening date. Everything in the simulation is fictional.

Three answers to the only question that mattered, as the newsroom held them on 15 October: an official estimate, a documented contract and an expert assessment, each with its evidence and a confidence that comes from how independent that evidence is.
Top: what each source said the reopening date would be, day by day. Bottom: the five days the paper led with the story, against the fifty-seven days readers needed its current state.
The Courier on the five days the bridge was news, each front page one projection of the story graph with the tracker beside it, and the fifty-seven days in between that readers needed it.
Three readers' graphs meet the story graph at shared anchors: the bridge, the footbridge, the bypass, a bus route and a stop. Green claims are current; grey ones have been superseded and are kept.
Hannah's graph meets the story graph: her home, her children's school, her routines and routes on the left, held on her device; the anchors both graphs share; the claims that reach her through them.
What Hannah received, as WhatsApp messages from the tracker: seven messages over seven weeks, each one about her route, each with its source.

One question an agent asks every morning: is the bridge open, and when will it be? Searching on its own, it reads six pages, spends about sixteen cents and finds the council's first page; asking the newsroom, it spends about two cents and is right.

Who paid, and where it went: £2,707 from 1,596 readers and businesses, three institutions and an agent; 60% to the Courier, which pays the reporter's base salary out of it, a 20% commission to the reporter, 10% to the evidence contributors, 10% to infrastructure and payments. The prices, volumes and split are assumptions written in the vault's build script.
The vault, view by view: twenty of its twenty-three views, in the Day theme, the nine added in version 0.2 outlined.
Revenue against cost, day by day, crossing on 5 November; and the same story with more or fewer followers, where fixed costs stay put and variable costs follow use.
Revenue by month over two years, by who paid: the town in October and November, institutions and agents after that, against a cost that is almost all in the first two months.
Revenue by month across twelve stories: stories in their first three months in blue, the long tail of older stories in orange, which grows with every story added.
The relief scheme without and with the tracker: when the budget was set, who heard about it, who was paid, and what it cost the council to process.
A simulated model query: when will it reopen, asked on 16 October, answered from the three live claims with citations, and the context the model would be given.
The story as an API: every endpoint a GET, every response a file in the vault.
Four themes, one set of tokens: the same view in Night, Day, Paper and Ember.
What the editor expected, and what the town paid for: five of twelve agreed; the town cared more about the bridge than the newsroom did.
